qs.q: A patient with end-stage renal disease presents with a normocytic anaemia and a normal platelet count, yet experiences prolonged bleeding times and clinical bleeding tendencies. What is the direct cause of the bleeding tendency in this patient?
qs.e: While reduced erythropoietin production causes normocytic anaemia in renal disease, uraemia specifically impairs platelet function, creating a bleeding tendency despite a normal circulating platelet count. Hypersplenism in liver disease, rather than renal disease, causes thrombocytopenia.
qs.s: Haematology & Blood Transfusion Pathology: MDS, Stem Cell Transplant: MCQs

qs.q: A patient with chronic kidney disease presents with fatigue and a normocytic anaemia alongside normal platelet counts, yet exhibits a bleeding tendency. What is the primary cause of the bleeding tendency in this uraemic patient?
o: Decreased synthesis of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors
qs.e: Uraemia from renal disease can impair platelet function, leading to a bleeding tendency despite having a normal platelet count. Reduced erythropoietin production causes the normocytic anaemia rather than the bleeding symptoms.
qs.s: Haematology & Blood Transfusion Pathology: MDS, Stem Cell Transplant: MCQs
